title: Objection Handling - Raw Notes (Standard Demo v1)
linked_artifacts: Drive: Benchmark Proof Points - Slides Inputs
Drive: Persona Briefs - Platform Eng vs ML Eng vs Security
content:
Working doc. Brain-dump style from AE/SE + PMM review. Not final wording. Keep claims within approved ranges; if unsure, say “we can validate in your environment” and offer eval.

Goal: quick responses + steer back to the demo narrative (reliability, latency/cost controls, deployment flexibility, observability). Also: what we SHOW live vs what we ONLY SAY.

Owners for final clean-up: Soojin (narrative), Markus (SE realism), Naomi (security language), Camila (approved wording).

---

0) Guardrails / meta guidance
- Don’t argue numbers. Use: “we publish/confirm ranges; final depends on model + tokens + context length + hardware + concurrency.”
- Prefer: “Here’s the control you get” over “here’s our magic.”
- If prospect wants vendor comparison: ask what success criteria is (p95 latency? $/1k tokens? time to deploy in VPC? audit logs?) then anchor to that.
- If the demo output varies: acknowledge nondeterminism; we mitigate with pinned model versions + prompt sets + regression checks.
- “What we show live” must be robust in demo tenant. Anything flaky: show screenshot or pre-record backup.

Live vs not-live (current)
- Live: streaming chat, tool calling / structured output, routing & fallback policy (forced failure), cost dashboard (token-level breakdown), error analysis + traces.
- Not-live / screenshot: deep kernel optimizations, some benchmark charts, private/on-prem install steps (unless a recorded clip).

---

1) “Why not just use <hyperscaler managed endpoints>?”
What they mean:
- They already have cloud commit + want one vendor.
- They don’t want another control plane.

Response angles (pick 1–2):
- Serving economics + controls: “Most managed endpoints optimize for generality; Redwood gives you explicit levers (batching/caching/quant profiles/routing) with visibility into cost per request/token.”
- Multi-environment: “Same API + console whether hosted today, dedicated next quarter, private/VPC later.” (Key: avoid re-platforming.)
- Reliability behavior: “You can define fallback policies explicitly (compatible model variant, region, capacity tier) and observe the impact.”

Suggested line: “If you’re happy with a single endpoint and default behavior, managed endpoints can be fine. Redwood is for teams who need predictable latency/cost and operational control across deployment modes.”

Follow-up Q to ask: “Are you optimizing for fastest procurement, or predictable p95 at scale + rollback/fallback control?”

Proof / show:
- Show routing policy page + a forced fallback demo (simulate primary capacity constrained -> fallback).

Competitive note:
- Be careful: don’t claim they can’t do X; claim we make it “simpler/more unified/observable.”

---

2) “Why not just call <LLM API provider> directly?”
What they mean:
- They want fast integration + don’t want to manage GPUs.

Response angles:
- Model flexibility + avoiding lock-in: “We support curated open models + can pin versions; you’re not stuck with one provider’s model roadmap.”
- Deployment flexibility: “You can start hosted, then move to dedicated/private for isolation/SLAs/regulatory.”
- Observability: “Token-level cost and latency, per route/model breakdown, rollouts with guardrails.”

If they say “But we like simplicity”:
- “Our hosted API is designed to be that simple—SDKs + streaming + structured output—while adding the ops layer teams usually build later.”

Proof / show:
- Show the same request running on 2 routes (e.g., ‘fast’ vs ‘cost-optimized’) with dashboards showing impact.

---

3) “We can self-host <open-source runtime>.”
What they mean:
- They have infra engineers and want control.

Response angles:
- Operating overhead: “The runtime is only part of the problem; the hard part is production operations: autoscaling, KV cache behavior under load, quota/rate limiting, multi-tenant isolation, dashboards, incident response.”
- Policy + rollouts: “Model version pinning, canaries/A-B, automatic fallback, regression checks tied to prompt sets.”
- “We can run in your VPC / on-prem” (if relevant) without them building control plane.

Suggested line: “If you want to own every layer and have a team for it, self-host can work. Teams choose Redwood when they want those controls without building and maintaining the full platform.”

Proof / show:
- Console rollout view + “rollback in 1 click” + error analysis + trace drill-down.

---

4) “Your benchmarks seem cherry-picked / not credible.”
Response:
- “Totally fair. We treat benchmarks as directional. The reliable way is to test your workload (prompt distribution, context length, concurrency). We’ll help you run a workload replay or quick eval.”
- “We can share methodology and safe ranges; no ‘one weird trick’ claims.”

Do NOT do:
- Don’t cite a single absolute number as universal.

Offer:
- “Let’s define a target SLO (p95 latency, throughput, $/request). We’ll run a controlled benchmark during eval.”

Link:
- Benchmark Proof Points - Slides Inputs (Drive). Keep within approved language.

---

5) “How do you handle reliability? We’ve seen LLM endpoints flake.”
Response angles:
- Routing/fallback: “Policy-driven routing with automated fallback to compatible model variants / regions / capacity tiers.”
- Graceful degradation: “We’d rather serve a slightly smaller model than error out.” (Confirm with prospect this is acceptable.)
- Observability: “You see errors by route/model, 5xx, throttles, and latency distributions. It’s not a black box.”

Live demo:
- Show forced fallback + show the event in dashboards (errors drop, latency impact visible).

Good question to ask:
- “What’s your acceptable degradation mode? Slower, smaller model, or hard fail?”

---

6) “What about output quality? Optimizations/quantization might degrade.”
Response angles:
- “We treat quality as a first-class metric. We recommend quantization profiles based on workload + can gate rollouts using evals/prompt sets.”
- “You can pin a model version and profile per route; change control is explicit.”
- “If quality matters more than cost, route policy can reflect that.”

Avoid:
- Overpromising “no quality loss.”

Offer:
- “We’ll set up a small eval harness with your prompts and show quality/cost tradeoffs.”

---

7) “Latency is good in your demo, but will it hold at our concurrency?”
Response:
- “The key is behavior under load (queueing, batching, cache hit rate). We can simulate concurrency and show p95/p99 + throttling behavior.”
- “Dedicated capacity gives predictability if you need guaranteed throughput.”

Ask:
- “Is your workload spiky? Do you need burst or steady-state?”

Proof:
- Show dashboards: latency percentile chart + throughput + batch size, if available.

---

8) “Your pricing is unclear / seems expensive.”
Notes:
- This came up in Slack. Decision: keep numbers out of deck. Use ranges + ‘drivers of cost’.

Response angles:
- Cost transparency: “We break down token costs per route/model; you can directly see what changed.”
- Levers: “Batching/caching/routing/quant profiles are explicit and measurable.”
- Packaging: “Hosted usage-based; Dedicated reserved; Private licensing + support.”

If procurement pushes for list price in first meeting:
- “We’ll provide a quote after we size the workload (tokens, model, latency target, regions). We can give a range today and tighten it in eval.”

Avoid:
- “We’re cheaper than X” without a scoped workload.

---

9) “Do you train on our data? What’s retention? What gets logged?” (SECURITY persona)
Use approved phrasing from Demo Tenant Security FAQ.

Draft answer:
- “We do not train foundation models on customer prompts/outputs.”
- “Retention and logging are configurable by deployment mode and contract. For the demo tenant, we use sanitized data and restricted access; logs are for operational debugging and are access-controlled.”
- “Private/VPC options support customer-managed networking and key management integrations.”

Be careful:
- Don’t invent specific retention durations here; point to FAQ + offer security review call.

If they ask about audit logs / SIEM:
- “We provide audit logs for administrative actions and access; integration options exist (details in security package).” (Need Naomi/Kevin to confirm exact scope.)

---

10) “Can you do SSO/SAML/RBAC?”
Response:
- “Yes—SSO/SAML for enterprise, RBAC for tenant access and admin actions. We can scope roles to demo tenant access as well.”

Follow-up:
- “Do you need SCIM provisioning? MFA enforcement? IP allowlists?” (Route to security package.)

---

11) “Where is data processed? We need EU-only.” (EMEA)
Response:
- “We support region selection and routing policies by region. For strict residency, Dedicated/Private options are typically the cleanest path.”

Demo reality check:
- Demo tenant may not be EU-only by default; if asked, don’t bluff. Offer to show policy controls + propose EU region in eval/POC.

Action item:
- Add an EMEA appendix slide? (Lukas asked.)

---

12) “We can’t send PHI/PCI. How do you support regulated workloads?”
Response:
- “Private deployment (VPC/on-prem) with customer-managed networking, key management integrations, and audit logs. We can align to your compliance requirements and security review process.”

Avoid:
- Claiming certification details in the room unless confirmed + current.

---

13) “What happens when a model changes under the hood? We’ve been burned.”
Response:
- “Model version pinning + explicit rollouts. You choose when to upgrade; we can canary/A-B and automatically rollback on regression signals.”

Live proof:
- Show pinned version in route config (if available in console).

---

14) “We need to run offline / air-gapped.”
Response:
- “We have private deployment options, including on-prem packages for regulated/air-gapped environments. We’ll scope hardware and update cadence.”

Parking lot:
- Need a clean one-pager of what’s supported in air-gapped mode (updates, model onboarding, telemetry). (Assign: Ethan/Priya?)

---

15) “What’s your SLA / support model?”
Response:
- “Hosted: standard uptime targets; Dedicated: SLA-backed uptime/latency targets; Private: enterprise support tiers. We’ll align SLA to tier.”

Avoid:
- Quoting exact SLA numbers unless slide is approved/current.

---

16) “Can we bring our own model? Custom weights?”
Response (draft):
- “We can support onboarding models depending on architecture and requirements. Many customers start with curated open models; for BYOM we’ll scope it in evaluation.”

Ask:
- “Is it a standard architecture? Any custom layers? What license constraints?”

Parking lot:
- Confirm internal policy on which models are supported in Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private.

---

17) “What about tool calling / structured output reliability?”
Response:
- “We support structured output patterns and tool calling; we recommend guardrails and validation. For critical workflows, we design prompts and validation together.”

Show:
- Live: structured JSON output example + server-side validation error path.

---

18) “We saw a 429 / throttling during trial. Is that normal?”
Response:
- “Rate limits and quotas are configurable. In demos we use safe defaults to avoid surprises; in trials we’ll size limits to your expected concurrency.”

Note:
- This is a common confusion point. Add a ‘what 429 means’ slide/FAQ snippet?

---

19) “What if the model output is different live vs expected?”
Response:
- “Some nondeterminism is inherent. For demos and regression checks we use pinned versions, known-good prompts, and—where needed—lower temperature. In production, we recommend evals + monitoring for drift.”

Suggested phrasing:
- “We don’t pretend LLMs are deterministic. We give you the tooling to manage it.”

---

20) “Is Redwood just a gateway? What’s actually differentiated?”
Response:
- “It’s a serving platform: optimized runtime + orchestration layer + operational tooling. The differentiation is predictable production serving: routing/fallback, cost/latency levers, rollouts, and deep observability.”

If they press:
- “Happy to go deep on runtime optimizations in a follow-up with engineering; in this call we’ll stay focused on the controls you’ll use day to day.”

---

21) “Vendor risk: you’re smaller than <big company>.”
Response angles:
- “We’re purpose-built for inference; faster iteration on serving economics. We offer Dedicated/Private to reduce operational risk and align support/SLAs.”
- “We can start with a small scoped evaluation with success criteria and exit plan.”

Avoid:
- Anything that sounds defensive.

---

22) “We need to see a POC plan, not just a demo.”
Response:
- “Great—let’s define success criteria and run a 2–3 week eval: workload replay, SLO targets, quality checks, and security review.”

Artifacts to prep:
- POC checklist (separate doc).

---

Competitive intel placeholders (needs cleanup; don’t share externally)
- Hyperscaler endpoints: strong integration + procurement; less transparent unit economics; multi-region complexity.
- LLM API providers: easy start; less deployment flexibility; limited control over fallbacks/version pinning.
- Self-host runtime: maximum control; highest ops burden; teams underestimate oncall + dashboards + rollouts.

Notes from field (unfiltered)

- “Security folks want specifics fast. Have the FAQ link ready and offer follow-up with security lead.”
- “If latency question comes up early, jump to the dashboard quickly—it builds trust.”
